title: Disaster policy faces a coverage-versus-intensity choice, with lower-income populations carrying large poverty and well-being losses
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11334, Coverage or Intensity of Support? Adaptive Social Protection to Reduce Disaster-Related Poverty
geography: 131 countries, with global estimates of disaster-related poverty and modeled adaptive social-protection expansion scenarios

poverty_risk.value: 25.6 million people are estimated to be at risk of poverty due to disasters, including 12.7 million facing extreme poverty

consumption_loss.value: disaster-related consumption losses are estimated at $758 billion

wellbeing_loss.value: well-being losses are estimated as equivalent to a uniform $1.143 trillion drop in consumption

observations.method: Global modeling of poverty, consumption and well-being losses from natural hazards, combined with adaptive social-protection policy scenarios.
observations.uncertainty: These are modeled global estimates that depend on hazard, poverty, exposure, consumption and welfare assumptions; they are not a contemporaneous disaster-loss census or respondent-level measurement.
observations.subgroup: People vulnerable to disaster-related poverty, people facing extreme poverty, lower-income populations, governments, social-protection systems and disaster-risk agencies.
observations.counterinterpretation: Modeled welfare-equivalent losses should not be read as cash losses to households or as a direct estimate of how many people would actually receive assistance.

denominator.unit: policy dimensions compared in the paper

coverage.value: coverage is the breadth of the population reached by a support measure

intensity.value: intensity is the extent of support received by each beneficiary

tradeoff.value: limited resources force governments to choose how to balance reaching more people with supporting each recipient more deeply

observations.method: Systematic comparison of modeled adaptive social-protection measures under alternative coverage and intensity expansions.
observations.uncertainty: Scenario results depend on transfer design, targeting, administrative feasibility, fiscal resources, hazard assumptions and implementation quality.
observations.subgroup: Potential beneficiaries, excluded households, existing transfer recipients, social-protection administrators and fiscal authorities.
observations.counterinterpretation: The coverage-intensity framing can omit delivery speed, dignity, access costs, grievance systems, informal support and whether benefits arrive before irreversible losses.

observations.period: 2026; modeled policy expansion across income groups

overall_pattern.value: total benefits are usually largest in scenarios with the most extensive coverage and intensity

expansion_path.value: the optimal expansion path differs by measure and country income group

lower_income_priority.value: prioritizing intensity while focusing on lower-income populations is generally most effective for reducing socio-economic disaster impacts

observations.method: Comparative scenario analysis by adaptive social-protection measure and country income group.
observations.uncertainty: The modeled optimum is not a universal program prescription; political targeting, administrative capacity and local price and hazard conditions can change the ranking.
observations.subgroup: Lower-income populations, existing beneficiaries, near-poor households, countries at different income levels and agencies allocating scarce disaster-response resources.
observations.counterinterpretation: Targeting intensity toward lower-income groups may leave many near-poor or newly affected households without timely help, creating legitimacy and social-cohesion risks.

denominator.unit: higher- and lower-income country groups compared in the policy scenarios

lower_income.value: lower-income countries benefit more strongly from early increases in coverage than higher-income countries

sequence.value: the right order of broadening reach and increasing support depends on country income and the measure being expanded

system_signal.value: adaptive protection is an institutional bridge joining disaster risk management, climate adaptation and social-protection delivery

observations.method: Income-group comparison of modeled adaptive social-protection expansion paths.
observations.uncertainty: The paper does not establish that modeled early coverage increases can be implemented quickly, accurately or equitably in every lower-income setting.
observations.subgroup: Lower-income countries, first-time beneficiaries, disaster-exposed households, local delivery institutions and international funders.
observations.counterinterpretation: Early coverage expansion without adequate benefit intensity or reliable delivery may create nominal inclusion without meaningful recovery capacity.

related_sources.claim: World Bank reproducibility package documenting the 131-country modeling frame, data sources, scenarios and computational verification.
World Bank Tokyo Disaster Risk Management Hub listing the 2026 adaptive social-protection publication.

boundary: This record adds an adaptive-social-protection route linking natural hazards to poverty, consumption room, well-being, coverage, benefit intensity, targeting, fiscal capacity and institutional delivery. It is modeled cross-country scenario evidence, not respondent-level data, a disaster-loss census, an implementation audit or proof that support arrives in time.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official World Bank working-paper PDF, World Bank reproducibility package and disaster-risk hub listing were reviewed for the 131-country frame, poverty and welfare estimates, coverage-intensity framework, income-group expansion paths and implementation boundaries.
